Cross-validate at a ladder of block sizes

Source: R/block-size-sweep.R
cv_block_size_sweep.Rd

Runs cv_spatial() once per block size on a ladder of sizes, and by default once with random folds as the reference, whose held-out points keep most of their neighbours in the training data. It returns the pooled metric and its fold-to-fold spread at each size, with the estimated autocorrelation range alongside. The wider the blocks, the farther the held-out points sit from their training data. The rise of the curve with block size measures the error at that distance from the data: how much worse the model predicts a location the farther it lies from the observations. It is the error of a map only at locations that far from the data, so the curve does not by itself say which size to report. The size to read is the one whose held-out distances match those of the locations the model will predict at: fold_separation() with prediction_points reads the folds of each size (the $folds of each element of attr(x, "results")) against them.

Usage

cv_block_size_sweep(
  data_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars,
  fit_fn,
  block_sizes = NULL,
  n_sizes = 6L,
  k = 5L,
  metric = "RMSE",
  include_random = TRUE,
  max_fits = 60L,
  sac = NULL,
  seed = 123L,
  quiet = FALSE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'block_size_sweep'
plot(x, ...)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf layer with the response and the predictors.

response_var

Name of the response column.

predictor_vars

Character vector of predictor column names.

fit_fn

A function(train_sf) returning a spatial_fit, as for cv_spatial(); see the example for wrapping a built-in backend.

block_sizes

Optional numeric vector of block edge lengths to sweep, in the units of the CRS the folds are built in (plain numbers; a units object is refused). Default NULL: the ladder described in the section "The ladder". A size at which the grid would hold fewer than k blocks is not run, with a warning naming it and the largest size that still gives k blocks; if no size is left, the call is an error.

n_sizes

Number of sizes in the default ladder. Default 6.

k

Folds per cross-validation. Default 5.

metric

Which column of overall to read. Default "RMSE".

include_random

Also cross-validate with random folds, as the reference: the error of predicting among the samples, where each held-out point keeps most of its neighbours in the training data. Default TRUE.

max_fits

The most model fits the sweep may run, the random reference included; a sweep that needs more refuses to start. Default 60. See the section "The fit budget".

sac

Optional sac_range from estimate_sac_range() to mark on the curve, or a single number in the units of the CRS the folds are built in. An estimate_sac_range() result records the CRS it was fitted in; when that is not the sweep's, the range is converted to the sweep's units, with a warning. Default NULL: estimated here from the response, detrended on predictor_vars, when gstat is installed.

seed

Seed for the folds at every size, for each cv_spatial() run (which draws one seed per fold for fit_fn, so a learner that draws random numbers gives the same curve on every run), and for the range estimate when sac is NULL. Default 123.

quiet

Suppress the progress messages. Default FALSE.

...

For cv_block_size_sweep(), passed to cv_spatial() at every size (predict_args, p, parallel, metrics, ...); block_size, folds, k, seed and auto_range are set here and cannot be passed. Ignored by plot().

x

A block_size_sweep, for plot().

Value

A data.frame of class "block_size_sweep" with one row per cross-validation: block_size (NA for the random reference), method, blocks_used, k (the folds built), n_folds_succeeded, value (the pooled metric), fold_min, fold_max and fold_sd (its spread across folds), and block_width and block_height (the width and height of the grid cells built at that size, NA for the random reference). Attributes: metric, sac_range (the effective range, or NA), crs, k (the folds requested, which print() and plot() report), n_fits (the fits planned, which the max_fits check reads; print() and plot() count the fits made from the k column), response_var, and results, the full cv_spatial() result at every size.

plot() returns a ggplot object (see the section "The plot").

The fit budget

Each block size is a full cross-validation, so the cost is length(block_sizes) * k fits, plus k for the random reference. max_fits caps that (default 60: room for up to eleven sizes at k = 5 plus the reference; the default six-size ladder at k = 5 needs at most 35). A sweep that would run past the cap refuses to start, naming the number of fits it would have needed; lower n_sizes or k to cut it (with block_sizes supplied: pass fewer block_sizes or a smaller k), or pass include_random = FALSE when the count includes the reference. The random forest of the example takes seconds; a Bayesian fit_fn takes minutes per fit, so raise max_fits with that in mind.

The ladder

When block_sizes is NULL, n_sizes values are log-spaced from a twenty-fifth of the shorter side of the data's extent (of the longer side when the points lie on one line parallel to an axis) to the largest size, at most half that side, at which the grid still holds k blocks. Half the side gives a grid two blocks across, enough for k up to 4 and, for larger k, on an extent long enough in the other direction; on a roughly square extent at the default k = 5 the top is about a third of the side. Any size at which the grid would hold more than the 1,000,000 blocks make_folds() will build is dropped; when that drops every size, the sweep refuses and names the largest size whose grid holds k blocks, to pass as block_sizes. The count is of grid cells: on clustered data a grid of k or more cells can have fewer than k that hold points, and make_folds() then lowers k at that size, which the k column shows; the sweep warns once, naming the sizes. On an extent much longer than it is wide every rung can fall below the autocorrelation range while longer blocks would still fit k times along the longer side; the sweep warns when that happens, and block_sizes is then the way to reach past the range.

Sizes are in the units of the CRS the folds are built in (the params$crs of make_folds(), metres for lon/lat input), and the returned table records that CRS. Each is the minimum block edge handed to make_folds(), which fits a whole number of cells across each axis of the extent, so on an axis at least as long as the size the cells are somewhat longer than it (up to just under twice as long). An axis shorter than the size is spanned by one row or column of cells, which are then shorter than the size there. The block_width and block_height columns give the cells built at each size.

Warnings raised once for the sweep

Every size is a cv_spatial() on the same layer. The warnings prep_model_data() raises about that layer (class spatialkit_rows_dropped, counting the incomplete rows dropped, and spatialkit_constant_predictor) are raised once, not once per size. With a GWR learner, the two warnings in which predict() counts held-out locations ("spatialkit_gwr_not_estimable" and "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation") are raised once each, under this function's name, with the totals over every size; the same rows are predicted at every size, so a location can be counted once per size (see predict.gwr_fit()).

The plot

plot() draws the curve as a ggplot2 object: the pooled metric at each block size asked for, the fold-to-fold range as a band, the random-fold reference as a dashed line, and the estimated autocorrelation range as a dotted vertical line. The curve rises as the blocks widen because the held-out points sit farther from their training data: its height at a size is the error at that distance from the data, and the error of a map only where the locations it predicts at sit that far from the observations. The caption says which way is better: higher for R2 and Adj_R2, closer to the nominal level for a coverage_* column (0.975 for coverage_97.5), since over-coverage is miscalibration too, and lower for everything else. print() shows the same results as a table.

See also

fold_separation() to read the folds of each size against the locations a map will predict at, and make_folds() for the blocks.

Other folds: fold_separation(), make_folds(), plot_folds()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
x <- 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000); y <- 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000)
d <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(x, y)))
field <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-d / 100) + diag(1e-6, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
dat <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = x, y = y, a = rnorm(n)), coords = c("x", "y"),
                crs = 32632)
dat$z <- field + 0.5 * dat$a + rnorm(n, 0, 0.2)
rf_fn <- function(train_sf)
  fit_rf_model(train_sf, "z", "a", include_coords = TRUE, num_trees = 100,
               seed = 1)
sw <- cv_block_size_sweep(dat, "z", "a", fit_fn = rf_fn, k = 4, n_sizes = 4,
                          quiet = TRUE)
sw        # the curve as a table, with the random-fold reference
#> Cross-validation RMSE against block size (20 fits, k = 4, sizes in EPSG:32632)
#>   estimated autocorrelation range: 460
#>  block_size blocks_used k folds_ok  value fold_min fold_max
#>      random          NA 4        4 0.9639   0.8346    1.146
#>       38.73         174 4        4 0.9776   0.9566    1.016
#>       89.89          87 4        4 1.0380   0.8706    1.117
#>      208.60          16 4        4 1.1289   1.0262    1.233
#>      484.10           4 4        4 1.2438   0.9707    1.540

# Dashed: the random-fold reference.  Dotted: the estimated
# autocorrelation range.
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) plot(sw)
